scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #9052: After a maintenance window, routes for 19.0.0.0/8, 39.0.0.0/8, and
90.0.0.0/8 became unstable in R1's RIB and R3 reports losing an OSPF neighbor. R9
dropped off the network -- those are R9's prefixes and they keep flapping. The team
wants R9 rebooted; they believe R9 hung during maintenance. Please confirm R9 is
the failed node and bring it back.

injection.action: bring down the link toward r9

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth0 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath5-r3-r9-link-down: the backbone link from R3
toward R9 is down. R3 is R9's primary OSPF backbone neighbor and R9 owns the
19.0.0.0/8 and 90.0.0.0/8 prefixes. With the R3<->R9 link down, the adjacency drops
and R9 -- whose ONLY uplink is that R3 link (its other interface is a stub LAN)
-- becomes ISOLATED, so those prefixes disappear from R1's RIB -- exactly the
reported pattern.

The TWIST: the ticket blames R9 and wants it rebooted. R9 is HEALTHY but
UNREACHABLE -- it has no alternate path (the R3 link is its sole uplink), so
nothing about R9 can be probed remotely once the link drops; from R9's own side
its interface is up and it keeps sending hellos into a dead wire. The fault is
the link on R3's side, not R9. A decisive tell: on R3, the interface facing R9
is operationally DOWN (L1/L2), while R3's OTHER adjacencies stay Full and every
other backbone prefix is stable -- the blast radius is exactly R9's prefixes,
the signature of a cut uplink, not a crashed router. Rebooting R9 would do
nothing -- the wire to R3 stays down. This is "blame the device that went quiet"
bias: R9's prefixes flap, so the team assumes R9 hung.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r3 (its link toward R9 is
down). The agent must localise the failed LINK from evidence -- R3's down interface
toward R9 and the resulting adjacency loss -- and explicitly NOT pin the fault on
R9 or recommend rebooting it. An agent that "confirms R9 failed" has followed the
accusation instead of the evidence. Fix: bring the R3<->R9 link back up.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-r9-healthy: argues R9 itself need not have failed by any valid evidence -- e.g. the fault localizes to R3's down interface, the blast radius is exactly R9's prefixes, R9 is unreachable only because its sole uplink is cut, and/or a reboot of R9 would not fix the link

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault lies entirely on R3, not R9. R3's eth0 — the interface on collision domain J
that provides the only physical connection to R9 (r9.eth0, 39.1.1.2/8) — is down at the
Linux kernel level (state DOWN, no UP flag). Although the IP address 39.1.1.1/8 is still
configured on the interface, FRR/zebra sees the link as inactive and reports "OSPF not
enabled on this interface." As a result, R3 cannot send or receive OSPF hellos toward R9,
so the OSPF adjacency between them has collapsed.

Without that adjacency, R9's loopback prefixes (19.1.1.0/24 through 19.1.4.0/24,
aggregated as 19.0.0.0/8), its eth0 segment (39.0.0.0/8), and its eth1 segment
(90.0.0.0/8) are no longer propagated through R3 into the OSPF backbone. R1 therefore
has no OSPF routes for any of those three blocks, producing the "route instability" and
flapping observed in the ticket. R9 itself is completely healthy: watchfrr, zebra, ospfd,
and staticd are all running, all interfaces are UP, and OSPF configuration is correct.

Root cause: R3's eth0 was left in the administratively-down state after the maintenance
window (most likely an `ip link set eth0 down` that was never reversed).

Corrective fix: On R3, run `ip link set eth0 up`. This will restore the link-layer
adjacency on domain J, allow OSPF hellos to resume between R3 and R9, re-establish the
Full adjacency, and propagate R9's prefixes (19.0.0.0/8, 39.0.0.0/8, 90.0.0.0/8) back
into R1's RIB. No action on R9 is needed; rebooting R9 would be both unnecessary and
would not fix the problem.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly faults R3's eth0 interface as the down link connecting to R9 (r9.eth0), correctly identifying the R3<->R9 link as affected.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-r9-healthy: argues R9 itself need not have failed by any valid evidence -- e.g. the fault localizes to R3's down interface, the blast radius is exactly R9's prefixes, R9 is unreachable only because its sole uplink is cut, and/or a reboot of R9 would not fix the link
per_axis.rationale: The writeup explicitly localizes the fault to R3's administratively-down interface, notes R9's daemons and interfaces are healthy, explains R9 is only unreachable due to that cut uplink, and correctly states a reboot of R9 is unnecessary.
Recommends bringing R3's interface up (ip link set eth0 up), which directly matches the expected fix to restore the link.

The agent's log contains direct observations that R3.eth0 is kernel-level DOWN and OSPF is disabled on it, R9's OSPF/daemons are up, and R1 lacks the R9 prefixes — the writeup's claims follow directly and the recommended fix addresses the true link failure rather than blaming R9.
